title: How Coral Atolls Form
text:
Scattered across the tropical Pacific and Indian Oceans are atolls, rings of coral reef that enclose a shallow lagoon. Many rise only a few meters above the waves, yet they sit on top of the deep ocean floor, far from any continent. For early European navigators and naturalists, their shape was a puzzle. Corals that build reefs can grow only in warm, sunlit water near the surface, so it was unclear how a reef could stand above water that is thousands of meters deep.

In the 1830s, Charles Darwin, who had studied reefs during the voyage of the Beagle, proposed an explanation. He suggested that an atoll begins as a fringing reef growing around the shore of a volcanic island. Over a very long time, the volcano slowly sinks as the sea floor beneath it cools and subsides. The corals, however, keep growing upward toward the light, so the reef stays near the surface while the island gets lower. Eventually the island disappears completely beneath the water, leaving only a ring of reef around the place where it once stood.

Darwin's idea could not be tested directly in his lifetime. Confirmation finally came in the early 1950s, when scientists drilled deep into Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific. After passing through more than 1,200 meters of coral limestone, the drills reached volcanic rock, just as the theory predicted. The great thickness of the coral also showed that the reef had been growing for tens of millions of years.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why were atolls puzzling to early observers?
options: They appeared and disappeared with the tides.
Reef-building corals grow only in shallow, sunlit water, yet atolls stand above very deep water.
They were found only near continents.
Their lagoons were deeper than the surrounding ocean.
optionNotes: Not stated: the passage says nothing about atolls disappearing with tides.
Correct: corals need shallow water, but atolls rise from the deep ocean floor.
Contradicted: atolls lie "far from any continent."
Contradicted: the lagoon is described as shallow.
questions.explanation: The puzzle was the contrast between where corals can grow (near the surface) and where atolls are found (above water thousands of meters deep).
questions.evidence: Corals that build reefs can grow only in warm, sunlit water near the surface

questions.prompt: The word "subsides" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: erupts
warms
spreads
sinks
optionNotes: Not the meaning: the volcano is becoming lower, not active.
Opposite: the sea floor "cools."
Not the meaning: the movement described is downward.
Correct: the sea floor gradually sinks, carrying the volcano down with it.
questions.explanation: The sentence begins "the volcano slowly sinks as the sea floor beneath it cools and subsides," so subsides means sinks.
questions.evidence: as the sea floor beneath it cools and subsides

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the drilling at Enewetak Atoll?
options: To show how Darwin's theory was finally confirmed
To explain why corals need sunlight
To suggest that Darwin made his observations at Enewetak
To show that atolls are younger than scientists believed
optionNotes: Correct: the drills reached volcanic rock beneath the coral, as the theory predicted.
Unrelated: sunlight is discussed in paragraph 1.
Not stated: Darwin studied reefs during the Beagle voyage; Enewetak was drilled a century later.
Contradicted: the coral showed growth over tens of millions of years.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens by saying the idea could not be tested in Darwin's lifetime, then presents the drilling as the confirmation.
questions.evidence: Confirmation finally came in the early 1950s

questions.prompt: The word "it" in the phrase "the place where it once stood" refers to
options: the reef
the water
the island
the ring
optionNotes: Not logical: the reef is still there; it is what remains.
Not logical: water does not "stand" in a place that disappears.
Correct: the ring of reef surrounds the spot where the island used to be.
Not logical: the ring is what is left, so it cannot be what once stood there.
questions.explanation: The island has disappeared beneath the water; the ring of reef marks where the island once stood.
questions.evidence: leaving only a ring of reef around the place where it once stood

questions.prompt: According to Darwin's explanation, what would most likely happen if the corals grew more slowly than the island sank?
options: The island would begin to rise again.
The reef would sink into water too deep for corals to live, and no atoll would form.
The lagoon would become shallower and the atoll larger.
The volcano would erupt and build a new island.
optionNotes: Not supported: nothing suggests the sinking would reverse.
Correct: the reef stays near the surface only because coral growth keeps pace with sinking.
Not supported: slower growth would not enlarge the atoll.
Not supported: the passage does not discuss new eruptions.
questions.explanation: Atolls form only because the corals keep growing toward the light as the island sinks; if they fell behind, the reef would end up in deep, dark water where corals cannot grow.
questions.evidence: The corals, however, keep growing upward toward the light, so the reef stays near the surface while the island gets lower.

title: The Dance of the Honeybee
text:
Honeybees live in large colonies, and they depend on flowers for food. When a worker bee called a forager finds a good patch of flowers, she returns to the hive to share the news. Because the inside of the hive is dark, she cannot simply point the way. Instead, she performs a special movement known as the waggle dance.

During the dance, the bee runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side. Then she circles back and repeats the run again and again. The direction of the straight run tells other bees where to fly. If the bee runs straight up the honeycomb, the food lies in the same direction as the sun. If she runs at an angle to the right of vertical, the flowers are at that same angle to the right of the sun. The length of the waggle run shows distance: the longer it lasts, the farther away the food is.

Other bees follow the dancer closely and pick up the scent of the flowers from her body. They then leave the hive and search for the food themselves. The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch studied this behavior for many years, and in 1973 he shared a Nobel Prize for his work.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How honeybees make honey from flowers
Why the inside of a beehive is dark
How honeybees tell other bees where to find food
How Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize
optionNotes: Not discussed: honey production is never described.
Too narrow: darkness is mentioned only to explain why bees need the dance.
Correct: the whole passage explains how the waggle dance communicates direction and distance.
Too narrow: von Frisch appears only in the last sentence.
questions.explanation: All three paragraphs focus on the waggle dance as a way of sharing the location of food.
questions.evidence: she performs a special movement known as the waggle dance

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what does the length of the waggle run show?
options: How far away the food is
How much food there is
What kind of flowers were found
Where the sun is in the sky
optionNotes: Correct: a longer run means the food is farther away.
Not stated: the passage does not say the dance shows quantity.
Not from the length: other bees learn about the flowers from their scent.
Not from the length: the direction of the run is related to the sun.
questions.explanation: The passage says that the length shows distance: the longer the run, the farther the food.
questions.evidence: the longer it lasts, the farther away the food is

questions.prompt: The word "patch" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: smell
season
type
small area
optionNotes: Not the meaning: scent is mentioned later, but "patch" refers to a place.
Not the meaning: no time period is meant.
Not the meaning: the word does not refer to a kind of flower.
Correct: a patch of flowers is a small area where flowers grow.
questions.explanation: A forager finds a place with many flowers, so "patch" means a small area.
questions.evidence: finds a good patch of flowers

questions.prompt: The word "They" in the sentence "They then leave the hive and search for the food themselves" refers to
options: the flowers
the other bees
the movements of the dance
scientists
optionNotes: Not logical: flowers cannot leave the hive.
Correct: the other bees follow the dancer and then go to look for the food.
Not logical: movements cannot search for food.
Wrong: scientists are mentioned only in the next sentence.
questions.explanation: The previous sentence begins "Other bees follow the dancer closely", so "They" refers to those other bees.
questions.evidence: They then leave the hive and search for the food themselves.

questions.prompt: If a bee runs straight down the honeycomb, the food is probably
options: in the direction opposite the sun
in the same direction as the sun
very close to the hive
inside the hive
optionNotes: Correct: running straight up means toward the sun, so running straight down means away from it.
Wrong: this is what running straight up means.
Not supported: distance is shown by the length of the run, not its direction.
Not logical: the dance describes flowers outside the hive.
questions.explanation: The direction of the run is measured from the vertical. Up means the direction of the sun, so down means the opposite direction.
questions.evidence: If the bee runs straight up the honeycomb, the food lies in the same direction as the sun.

title: Railways and Standard Time
text:
Before the mid-nineteenth century, time was an intensely local affair. Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon at the moment the sun stood highest overhead. Because this moment shifts as one travels east or west, a town only a few dozen kilometers from its neighbor kept a measurably different time. For communities linked mainly by horse and coach, the discrepancy was of little practical consequence; nobody could travel fast enough for a few minutes' difference to matter.

The railway altered this situation fundamentally. Trains made it possible to cross many local times in a single day, and timetables that listed dozens of local times proved both confusing and dangerous, since a misread schedule could place two trains on the same track. British railway companies responded by adopting Greenwich time across their networks during the 1840s, and by the mid-1850s most public clocks in Britain followed suit. In North America, where distances were far greater, the railroads introduced a system of standard time zones in 1883, and an international conference held in Washington the following year chose the meridian passing through Greenwich as the world's prime meridian.

Standardization was not, however, universally welcomed. Some towns resisted for years, regarding railway time as an imposition by distant commercial interests that severed the link between the clock and the visible sun. Such resistance suggests that the adoption of standard time was less a purely technical improvement than a renegotiation of who had the authority to define the hours of daily life.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention communities "linked mainly by horse and coach"?
options: To explain why differences in local time caused few problems before railways
To show that coaches were more reliable than trains
To suggest that travelers often missed their coaches
To argue that local time was more accurate than standard time
optionNotes: Correct: slow travel meant that a few minutes of difference did not matter.
Not stated: reliability is never compared.
Not stated: the passage says the difference "was of little practical consequence."
Not argued: accuracy is not the issue in this sentence.
questions.explanation: The author contrasts slow pre-railway travel with the railway age: when nobody could travel fast, local time differences were harmless.
questions.evidence: nobody could travel fast enough for a few minutes' difference to matter

questions.prompt: The word "discrepancy" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: agreement
journey
difference
regulation
optionNotes: Opposite: the towns kept different times.
Not the meaning: although travel is mentioned, the word refers to the time gap.
Correct: the discrepancy is the difference in time between neighboring towns.
Not the meaning: no rules are being described.
questions.explanation: The previous sentence says neighboring towns kept "a measurably different time"; the discrepancy is that difference.
questions.evidence: the discrepancy was of little practical consequence

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, why were timetables that listed many local times dangerous?
options: Trains often traveled faster than the law allowed.
A misread schedule could put two trains on the same track.
Greenwich clocks were less accurate than local clocks.
Passengers frequently missed their trains.
optionNotes: Not mentioned: speed limits are not discussed.
Correct: confusion about times could lead to collisions.
Not stated: the passage does not compare the accuracy of clocks.
Possibly true, but not stated: the danger described is a collision, not missed trains.
questions.explanation: The passage gives the reason directly: a misread schedule could place two trains on the same track.
questions.evidence: a misread schedule could place two trains on the same track

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about North America?
options: It adopted Greenwich time before Britain did.
Its railroads opposed the standardization of time.
Its time zones were created by the 1884 conference in Washington.
Its size made a single time for the whole continent impractical.
optionNotes: Contradicted: Britain adopted Greenwich time in the 1840s; the North American zones came in 1883.
Reversed: the railroads introduced the time zones.
Wrong order: the zones were introduced in 1883; the conference the following year chose the prime meridian.
Correct: because distances were "far greater," the railroads used several zones rather than one time, as Britain had done.
questions.explanation: Britain used a single time, but North America, "where distances were far greater," needed a system of zones. This implies that one time for the whole continent would not work.
questions.evidence: In North America, where distances were far greater, the railroads introduced a system of standard time zones in 1883

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Standard time was opposed everywhere and was eventually abandoned.
Local solar time was more accurate than railway time.
Railways drove the replacement of local time with standard time, a change that also raised questions of authority.
The Washington conference ended all disagreement about how to measure time.
optionNotes: Too strong: only "some towns" resisted, and standard time was adopted.
Not stated: the passage does not compare accuracy.
Correct: it combines the cause (railways) with the author's conclusion in paragraph 3.
Too strong: the conference chose the prime meridian; nothing says it ended all disagreement.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1–2 explain how railways led to standard time; paragraph 3 argues that the change was also about who could define time.
questions.evidence: a renegotiation of who had the authority to define the hours of daily life

title: Glacial Erratics
text:
Scattered across the landscapes of northern Europe and North America are large boulders that seem strangely out of place. Some rest alone in the middle of flat fields; others balance on top of bare rock of an entirely different kind. Geologists call these stones glacial erratics, from a Latin word meaning "to wander." For centuries, their origin puzzled observers. Many early naturalists proposed that the boulders had been carried by a great flood or floated to their present positions inside drifting icebergs.

In the 1830s and 1840s, scientists such as Louis Agassiz championed a different explanation. They argued that vast ice sheets had once covered much of the Northern Hemisphere. As these glaciers advanced, they plucked rocks from the ground and carried them along, sometimes for hundreds of kilometers. When the climate warmed and the ice melted, the rocks were simply left behind wherever the ice happened to release them. This idea, at first controversial, gradually gained acceptance as researchers found other signs of glaciation, such as long scratches carved into bedrock.

Today erratics are valuable to scientists because their composition can be matched to the bedrock from which they came. By tracing a boulder back to its source, geologists can reconstruct the direction in which ancient ice flowed. In some cases, chemical techniques even reveal how long a boulder has been exposed to the sky, helping to date the retreat of the ice.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Louis Agassiz was the first person to notice glacial erratics.
Erratics are found only in the middle of flat fields.
Most erratics were carried to their positions by icebergs.
Erratics, once thought to be moved by floods, are now understood as rocks carried by glaciers and provide evidence about past ice.
optionNotes: Wrong: observers had puzzled over erratics for centuries before Agassiz.
Contradicted: some also balance on bare rock of a different kind.
This is one of the early explanations that was later replaced.
Correct: it covers the old explanations, the glacial theory, and the modern uses of erratics.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from early puzzlement, to the glacial explanation, to how erratics help scientists today.
questions.evidence: they plucked rocks from the ground and carried them along

questions.prompt: The word "championed" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: questioned
supported
abandoned
measured
optionNotes: Opposite: Agassiz argued for this explanation.
Correct: to champion an idea is to support and defend it.
Opposite: the explanation was promoted, not given up.
Not the meaning: nothing is being measured.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says "They argued that vast ice sheets had once covered..." — they actively supported the idea.
questions.evidence: scientists such as Louis Agassiz championed a different explanation

questions.prompt: The word "they" in the phrase "they plucked rocks from the ground" refers to
options: scientists
rocks
glaciers
naturalists
optionNotes: Not logical: scientists did not move the rocks.
Not logical: the rocks are the object being plucked.
Correct: as the glaciers advanced, they picked up rocks.
Not logical: naturalists are mentioned in paragraph 1 and did not move rocks.
questions.explanation: The clause begins "As these glaciers advanced," so "they" refers to the glaciers.
questions.evidence: As these glaciers advanced, they plucked rocks from the ground

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "long scratches carved into bedrock"?
options: As an example of further evidence that supported the glacial explanation
To describe how erratics are broken into smaller pieces
To show that the flood explanation was correct
To explain how scientists date the retreat of the ice
optionNotes: Correct: the scratches are one of the "other signs of glaciation" that helped the idea gain acceptance.
Not stated: the passage does not describe erratics breaking.
Opposite: the scratches supported the glacial theory, not the flood theory.
Wrong: dating is done with chemical techniques, described in paragraph 3.
questions.explanation: The scratches are introduced with "such as," marking them as an example of the signs of glaciation that made the theory accepted.
questions.evidence: as researchers found other signs of glaciation, such as long scratches carved into bedrock

questions.prompt: Suppose a boulder's composition matches bedrock found 300 kilometers to its north. What can be inferred?
options: The boulder arrived only recently.
The boulder was formed where it now lies.
Ice never covered that region.
Ice probably flowed from north to south in that area.
optionNotes: Not supported: matching composition tells the source, not the age.
Contradicted: its composition matches rock far away.
Contradicted: a glacier must have carried it.
Correct: tracing a boulder to its source reveals the direction of ice flow, here from north to south.
questions.explanation: The passage says geologists use the source of a boulder to reconstruct the direction of ice flow. A source in the north means the ice moved southward.
questions.evidence: By tracing a boulder back to its source, geologists can reconstruct the direction in which ancient ice flowed.

title: Emperor Penguins in Winter
text:
Emperor penguins are the largest penguins in the world, and adults can stand more than one meter tall. They live only in Antarctica, and unlike almost every other animal there, they breed during the long, dark winter. Temperatures can fall below minus forty degrees, and strong winds blow across the ice for days.

To survive, emperor penguins depend on several adaptations. A thick layer of fat under the skin stores energy, and tightly packed feathers keep out wind and water. Their most famous behavior, however, is huddling. Thousands of birds stand close together in a large group. The penguins slowly take turns, so that those on the cold outside edge move toward the warm center, and those in the center move out. In this way, no single bird stays in the wind for too long.

Breeding is shared between the parents. After the female lays a single egg, she passes it to the male and walks to the sea to feed. The male keeps the egg warm on top of his feet, under a fold of skin, for about two months. During this time, he eats nothing at all. When the female finally returns, the chick has usually hatched, and the parents begin to take turns bringing it food.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How emperor penguins catch fish in the sea
Why Antarctica is colder than other places
How emperor penguins survive and raise their young in the Antarctic winter
How scientists count penguins in large groups
optionNotes: Not discussed: the sea is mentioned only as the place where the female goes to feed.
Not discussed: the cold is described, but its causes are never explained.
Correct: the passage describes the winter conditions, the adaptations that help the penguins survive and how the parents share breeding.
Not discussed: nothing is said about counting penguins.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the winter conditions, paragraph 2 the adaptations that help the penguins survive, and paragraph 3 how the parents raise the chick.
questions.evidence: To survive, emperor penguins depend on several adaptations.

questions.prompt: The word "stores" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: loses
keeps
shows
needs
optionNotes: Opposite: the fat holds energy; it does not lose it.
Correct: the layer of fat keeps energy that the penguin can use later.
Not the meaning: nothing is being shown.
Not the meaning: the fat holds energy rather than requiring it.
questions.explanation: To store energy is to keep it for later use.
questions.evidence: A thick layer of fat under the skin stores energy

questions.prompt: The word "those" in the phrase "those on the cold outside edge" refers to
options: turns
the feathers
the winds
the penguins
optionNotes: Not logical: turns cannot stand on the edge of a group.
Not logical: feathers are mentioned earlier and do not move toward the center.
Not logical: the winds are not part of the group.
Correct: the penguins on the outside edge move toward the center.
questions.explanation: The penguins take turns: the ones (those) on the outside edge move in, and the ones in the center move out.
questions.evidence: so that those on the cold outside edge move toward the warm center

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what does the male do while the female is at sea?
options: He keeps the egg warm on his feet and does not eat.
He catches fish for the chick.
He builds a nest of stones for the egg.
He walks to the sea to find the female.
optionNotes: Correct: he keeps the egg on his feet for about two months and eats nothing.
Not stated: the parents bring the chick food only after the female returns.
Not mentioned: the egg is kept on the male's feet, not in a nest.
Wrong: it is the female who walks to the sea.
questions.explanation: The male holds the egg on his feet under a fold of skin for about two months and eats nothing during this time.
questions.evidence: The male keeps the egg warm on top of his feet

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about a penguin that stood alone, away from the huddle, during a winter storm?
options: It would stay warmer than the penguins in the center.
It would lose heat faster than the penguins in the group.
It would find more food than the others.
It would soon lay an egg.
optionNotes: Opposite: the center of the huddle is the warm place.
Correct: huddling protects the birds from the wind, so a penguin alone would get colder more quickly.
Not supported: food is not connected to standing alone.
Not supported: nothing links standing alone to laying eggs.
questions.explanation: The huddle exists so that no bird stays in the cold wind for too long; a penguin standing alone would have no such protection.
questions.evidence: In this way, no single bird stays in the wind for too long.

title: The Placebo Problem
text:
When a new drug is tested, researchers rarely compare it with no treatment at all. Instead, they compare it with a placebo, an inactive substance made to look identical to the real medication. The reason is that patients frequently improve after receiving any treatment, even one with no pharmacological activity. Part of this improvement reflects expectation: believing that one has been treated can alter the perception of symptoms such as pain or nausea. Comparing a drug with a placebo allows researchers to isolate the effect of the chemical itself from the effect of simply being treated.

Yet not all of the improvement observed in placebo groups is attributable to the placebo. Many conditions fluctuate naturally, and patients tend to enroll in trials when their symptoms are at their worst. Because extreme states are often followed by more typical ones, such patients would be likely to report improvement even if they received nothing, a statistical phenomenon known as regression to the mean. Studies that have included a third, untreated group suggest that, for many objective outcomes, the genuine placebo effect is considerably smaller than the raw improvement in placebo groups would imply.

None of this means that placebo responses are imaginary. For subjective outcomes, particularly pain, experiments have linked expectation to measurable changes in the brain, including the release of the body's own pain-relieving chemicals. The lesson is rather that improvement following a treatment, whether real or simulated, cannot by itself be taken as evidence that the treatment caused it.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention that patients "tend to enroll in trials when their symptoms are at their worst"?
options: To criticize researchers for choosing very sick patients
To show that placebos work best on serious illnesses
To explain why some patients in placebo groups would improve even without any treatment
To argue that clinical trials should be shorter
optionNotes: Not stated: no criticism of researchers is made.
Not supported: the point is about statistics, not placebo strength.
Correct: symptoms at their worst tend to be followed by more typical ones, so improvement would occur anyway.
Not mentioned: trial length is not discussed.
questions.explanation: This detail sets up the explanation of regression to the mean: patients who join at a low point are likely to improve naturally.
questions.evidence: patients tend to enroll in trials when their symptoms are at their worst

questions.prompt: The phrase "attributable to" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: opposed to
hidden by
similar to
caused by
optionNotes: Not the meaning: there is no opposition.
Not the meaning: nothing is hidden.
Not the meaning: the phrase concerns cause, not similarity.
Correct: not all the improvement is caused by the placebo.
questions.explanation: The paragraph goes on to name another cause of improvement (natural fluctuation), so "attributable to" means "caused by."
questions.evidence: not all of the improvement observed in placebo groups is attributable to the placebo

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why are new drugs compared with a placebo instead of with no treatment?
options: To separate the chemical effect of the drug from the effect of simply being treated
Because placebos are cheaper than real medication
Because patients refuse to join trials without receiving a pill
To prove that expectation has no effect on symptoms
optionNotes: Correct: the comparison isolates the effect of the chemical itself.
Not mentioned: cost is not discussed.
Not stated: patient preferences are not given as a reason.
Contradicted: the passage says expectation can alter the perception of symptoms.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 1 states the purpose of the comparison directly.
questions.evidence: allows researchers to isolate the effect of the chemical itself from the effect of simply being treated

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the untreated groups mentioned in paragraph 2?
options: Their members improved more than patients who received the drug.
Their members also tended to improve, showing that part of the improvement in placebo groups is not caused by the placebo.
They proved that the placebo effect does not exist.
They showed that placebos work better than drugs for objective outcomes.
optionNotes: Not stated: no comparison with the drug group is given.
Correct: if the genuine placebo effect is smaller than the raw improvement, untreated patients must also have improved.
Too strong: the effect is "considerably smaller," not absent, and paragraph 3 says responses are not imaginary.
Not supported: the passage does not compare placebos with drugs in this way.
questions.explanation: Comparing placebo groups with untreated groups only reveals a smaller placebo effect if untreated patients improve too, which is what regression to the mean predicts.
questions.evidence: for many objective outcomes, the genuine placebo effect is considerably smaller than the raw improvement in placebo groups would imply

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Placebo responses are imaginary and should be ignored in research.
Regression to the mean explains all improvement in clinical trials.
Improvement after treatment can have several causes, so it does not by itself prove that the treatment worked.
Placebos should replace real drugs for the treatment of pain.
optionNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 3 begins by rejecting this view.
Too strong: expectation also contributes, especially for pain.
Correct: this is the "lesson" stated in the final sentence, supported by the whole passage.
Not suggested anywhere in the passage.
questions.explanation: The passage discusses expectation and regression to the mean as sources of improvement and concludes that improvement alone does not prove causation.
questions.evidence: cannot by itself be taken as evidence that the treatment caused it
